cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Missing tenant admin authorization check when truncating a partitioned topic

credits.value: Mingsheng Lin of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Xingchen Chen of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Qixu Liu of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS

descriptions.value:
The Apache Pulsar broker admin REST API provides a truncate operation for persistent topics (DELETE /admin/v2/persistent/{tenant}/{namespace}/{topic}/truncate). Truncating a topic moves all subscription cursors of the topic to the end of the topic and deletes the topic's inactive ledgers. Truncating a non-partitioned topic, or a single partition addressed by its partition name, correctly requires the tenant admin role or the superuser role. When the operation is requested for the name of a partitioned topic, the broker does not apply this tenant admin check to the caller. Instead, it truncates each partition using the broker's own internal admin client, which authenticates with the broker's configured client credentials rather than the caller's identity. Each per-partition truncate request is still checked for the tenant admin role or the superuser role, but against the broker's internal identity instead of the caller. The partitions are therefore truncated only when the broker's configured client role is a superuser or an admin of the target tenant, which is the usual configuration when authorization is enabled.

As a result, when that condition holds, an authenticated user who is not a tenant admin can truncate any partitioned topic on which the user has lookup permission. Caller authentication and lookup permission alone are not sufficient: if the broker's internal identity lacks tenant admin or superuser authorization for the target tenant, the per-partition requests are rejected. With the default authorization provider, lookup permission is granted by produce or consume permission on the topic or its namespace. A user with no permissions on the topic cannot trigger the issue. This impact analysis assumes that Pulsar has been configured with the default authorization provider. For custom authorization providers, the impact could be different.

Truncating a partitioned topic this way moves the cursors of all subscriptions on every partition to the end of the topic, so any unacknowledged backlog is skipped and is no longer delivered to consumers. It also deletes eligible older ledgers of each partition regardless of the namespace's configured retention policy, so messages stored in those ledgers can be permanently lost. The ledger currently being written is not deleted by the truncate operation. The issue does not allow reading message contents or changing permissions or configuration, and it does not give access to topics on which the user has no lookup permission.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately can reduce exposure by restricting network access to the broker's admin REST API (/admin/v2) to trusted administrative clients.

cna.title: Penpot: Share-link page-scope escalation: a share-link holder reads pages outside the link's authorized scope via the get-page RPC command

descriptions.value: Penpot is an open-source design and prototyping platform. Prior to 2.18.0, the get-page RPC accepts a share-link permission object with blanket read access but does not verify that the caller-selected page-id belongs to the link's authorized pages set. An attacker with both a valid share link and the attacker's own authenticated Penpot session can retrieve the complete shape and design data of another page in the same file when its identifier is known, because get-page requires authentication. The related get-file-fragment RPC also permits share-link access without mapping fragments to authorized pages. This issue is fixed in version 2.18.0.

cna.title: Console-operator: streams for apache kafka console: cross-namespace kafkauser secret exfiltration via confused deputy

workarounds.value:
1. Restrict Console CR RBAC — remove create/update verbs on consoles.console.streamshub.github.com from tenant-facing roles. Only trusted cluster administrators should manage Console CRs.
2. Audit existing Console CRs — review all Console CRs for kafkaUser.namespace fields pointing outside the CR's own namespace.
3. Network policy (defense-in-depth) — apply NetworkPolicy to restrict operator pod egress.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to enforce strict same-namespace boundary validation on KafkaUser credentials namespace references in Console Operator custom resources to prevent cross-namespace Secret reads: upgrade to the fixed Console Operator builds, which enforce an assertNamespaceAllowed() guard with a same-namespace default check when reading KafkaUser namespace configuration, closing all 2 injection vectors (Console custom resource namespace manipulation, cross-namespace Secret reference). Until patched, this is a concern on Kubernetes clusters running Console Operator where non-admin users have create or update permissions on Console custom resources, so Remove create and update permissions on Console custom resources from tenant roles and audit existing custom resources for kafkaUser.namespace values pointing outside their own namespace. As a compensating measure, Configure Kubernetes API server audit logging to record Console custom resource modifications and cross-namespace Secret read operations performed by the operator service account. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying confused deputy cross-namespace access defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-711 Admission Controller Policy Enforcement (OPA/Gatekeeper/Kyverno) (high)

descriptions.value: The StreamsHub Console operator acts as a confused deputy: a Kubernetes tenant with permission to create a Console custom resource can set spec.kafkaClusters[].credentials.kafkaUser.namespace to any namespace. The operator, running with cluster-wide Secrets RBAC, reads the victim-namespace KafkaUser Secret (SASL credentials or TLS private keys) and writes the plaintext material into a Secret in the attacker's namespace. No same-namespace check or allowlist exists anywhere in the code path.

cna.title: Langflow: OS command injection (RCE) via arbitrary command in MCP stdio server configuration

descriptions.value: Langflow is a tool for building and deploying AI-powered agents and workflows. Before Langflow 1.10.3, the MCP stdio transport launched whatever command / args a user put in an MCP server configuration, with no allowlist and (before 1.10.3) wrapped in bash -c "exec {command} ...". Any user able to reach the MCP server settings ("Settings → MCP Servers → Add MCP Server", POST/PATCH /api/v2/mcp/servers/{server_name}) or to build a flow with the MCP Tools component could add a "server" whose command is an arbitrary OS command (touch, rm -rf, a reverse shell, ...). The command runs on the Langflow host as the Langflow process user as soon as Langflow tries to connect to the server (listing servers, loading tools, running the flow) — even when the UI then reports that the stdio server failed to start. With the default LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=true, GET /api/v1/auto_login hands out a token without credentials, so on an exposed instance running the default configuration this is reachable without an account. AUTO_LOGIN is documented as a development-only setting; with it disabled, any authenticated (non-admin) user can exploit it. This issue is fixed in Langflow 1.10.3, langflow-base 0.10.3, and lfx 1.10.3.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.5.0, which fixes the issue.

descriptions.value:
Summary



Before version 0.9.0, the HTTP/1 upstream path in pingora-proxy passed the downstream request through upstream_request_filter and wrote it to the upstream without removing the client's Connection header, other hop-by-hop headers, or the headers Connection nominated, although RFC 9110 Section 7.6.1 requires intermediaries to remove them. The HTTP/2 upstream path already removed Connection and related HTTP/1-specific headers. A client could therefore nominate a header that the application adds in upstream_request_filter (for example, Connection: keep-alive, X-Forwarded-For). A downstream HTTP/1 intermediary that honors Connection would then strip the Pingora-added header before it reached the origin.




Impact



Specifically affects chained deployments where an HTTP/1 intermediary between Pingora and the origin processes Connection nominations (for example, Go's net/http/httputil.ReverseProxy) and the origin trusts headers added by that intermediary (for example, X-Forwarded-For for IP-based authorization). A remote, unauthenticated attacker can have those headers removed, potentially bypassing authorization. The reporter demonstrated access to an IP-restricted endpoint using X-Forwarded-For for IP validation on the origin. This is the same class of issue as CVE-2022-31813 in Apache HTTP Server.




Note that Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as no such chained deployment as described above exists with internal Pingora services, and Connection headers are sanitized before arriving at Pingora gateways.



Mitigation:

  *  

Upgrade to pingora 0.9.0 or later. By default, Pingora now removes hop-by-hop and Connection-nominated headers from upstream requests, and rejects requests whose Connection header nominates Host, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Proto, or a pseudo-header. This is controlled by PeerOptions::http_upstream_request_policy (HttpUpstreamRequestPolicy). Fix commits:  https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/commit/28c18e6b6b04dd0bd937234e5950049e6d74cded ,  https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/commit/ca23f1668eca8e78be7ba62ef0edbd458b40eeee 


  *  

Do not use HttpUpstreamRequestPolicy::preserve() if the origin relies on headers added by Pingora; it restores the old passthrough behavior.


  *  

If you cannot upgrade: in upstream_request_filter, remove the Connection header and every header it nominates before adding trusted headers.

cna.title: Predictable Media Stream Pre-Shared Key Vulnerability in TP-Link Tapo C325WB

descriptions.value: CAPEC-115 Authentication Bypass

TP-Link Tapo
C325WB V2 generates the pre-shared key used by its local media streaming
service with a time-seeded pseudo-random number generator, making the key
predictable and recoverable. An unauthenticated attacker on the adjacent
network can recover the key and authenticate to the media streaming service
without valid user credentials. 









Successful
exploitation may allow an unauthenticated adjacent-network attacker to access
and take over live video and audio streams, compromising the confidentiality
and integrity of camera media.

cna.title: Microsoft UFO: Arbitrary code execution in `run_shell` via `explorer.exe` argument injection

descriptions.value: Microsoft UFO is an open-source framework for intelligent automation across devices and platforms. Prior to 3.0.9, the run_shell tool in the CommandLineExecutor component of ufo/client/mcp/local_servers/cli_mcp_server.py validates only the first token of the bash_command parameter and permits explorer.exe. On Windows, explorer.exe delegates its following path argument to ShellExecute, so an attacker-influenced agent call can launch an arbitrary executable or script as the desktop user even though the subprocess uses shell=False. Exploitation depends on a user running an affected agent workflow and on inducing the tool call, but successful execution can access or modify that user's files, tokens, and sessions. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.9.

cna.title: Kiota: Code injection through doc-comment delimiter reformation in Kiota Java and PHP generators

descriptions.value: Kiota is an OpenAPI based HTTP Client code generator. From 0.5.0 until 1.35.0, Kiota's Java and PHP documentation-comment sanitizers delete block-comment terminators rather than neutralizing them, allowing overlapping characters to reform a terminator and place attacker-controlled OpenAPI text outside a generated documentation comment. The Java sanitizer also removes non-ASCII characters after deleting terminators, which can create a new terminator during normalization. Exploitation requires a developer or build pipeline to generate source from the malicious description and then compile and load the Java output or load the PHP output, after which injected code executes in the consuming application or build environment context. The version range is based on the Java defect and does not assert that PHP generation existed in every affected release. This issue is fixed in version 1.35.0.

supportingMedia.value:
Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in ash-project ash_typescript allows an unauthenticated attacker to read internal Elixir terms from an RPC error response by provoking an error the error builder has no dedicated clause for.

AshTypescript.Rpc.ErrorBuilder.build_error_response/1 in lib/ash_typescript/rpc/error_builder.ex renders a pipeline error term that matches no specific clause with inspect/1 and places the result in details.error of the client-facing error. Ash exceptions take a separate path in AshTypescript.Rpc.Errors where unhandled cases are redacted behind an errorId, but these fallbacks have no redaction, so whatever the term carries reaches the HTTP or channel response. Two request paths hand it such terms: a struct-typed action argument with an invalid nested value, where cast_map_to_struct/2 in lib/ash_typescript/rpc/input_formatter.ex throws the raw Ash.Type cast error into the builder, and field selection on a generic action that returns a primitive, where format_field_type/1 inspects the full Ash.Info.Manifest.Type struct into vars.returnType. Resource module names in vars.resource are not treated as sensitive and are out of scope.

This issue affects ash_typescript: from 0.1.0 before 0.19.1.

supportingMedia.value:
1. Error funnel. AshTypescript.Rpc.run_action/3 runs the request through Pipeline.parse_request/3, execute_ash_action/1 and process_result/2. Any {:error, reason} from these goes to error_response/1, which calls AshTypescript.Rpc.ErrorBuilder.build_error_response/1 with the raw reason term.

2. Unredacted fallbacks. build_error_response/1 has clauses for the error tuples the pipeline is expected to emit. A two-tuple whose first element is an atom but matches no clause is rendered as field_validation_error with details.error set to inspect(error), and any other term becomes unknown_error with details.error set to inspect(other). Ash exceptions never reach these clauses because AshTypescript.Rpc.Errors handles them and redacts unhandled ones behind an errorId, so only this path has no redaction.

3. Reachable triggers. AshTypescript.Rpc.InputFormatter.cast_map_to_struct/2 throws the raw Ash.Type.cast_input/3 error, a keyword list, when a struct-typed argument fails to cast, and format/6 turns the throw into {:error, term} for the funnel. Separately, requesting fields on a generic action whose return type is a primitive produces an {:invalid_field_selection, :primitive_type, return_type, ...} tuple whose return_type is formatted by format_field_type/1, which inspects the whole Ash.Info.Manifest.Type struct, constraints and decoration included, into vars.returnType.

cna.title: Authorization bypass through a user-controlled key in the Amazon Q Business Lambda hook sample in QnABot on AWS

descriptions.value: CAPEC-1 Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs

Authorization bypass through a user-controlled key in the optional Amazon Q Business Lambda hook sample ( q-business-lambda-hook https://github.com/aws-solutions-library-samples/qnabot-on-aws/blob/main/source/docs/lambda_hooks/README.md ), available with QnABot on AWS versions 7.0.0 through 7.4.5, might allow an authenticated remote user to read arbitrary Amazon S3 objects in the deploying AWS account. This sample solution provides an example Lambda hook and requires separate, manual deployment and additional setup. It is not deployed automatically with QnABot. Customers who have not deployed this optional sample hook are not affected and do not need to take action. 



To remediate this issue, affected customers should update the QnABot on AWS stack to version 7.4.6 or later and then redeploy the Amazon Q Business Lambda hook sample stack. Updating the QnABot on AWS stack alone does not deliver the fix.

cna.title: Microsoft UFO: Authenticated Android shell command injection in Mobile MCP type_text and launch_app

descriptions.value: Microsoft UFO is an open-source framework for intelligent automation across devices and platforms. Prior to 3.0.10, the type_text and launch_app tools in ufo/client/mcp/http_servers/mobile_mcp_server.py pass the authenticated caller-controlled text and package_name parameters into adb shell command argument positions without comprehensive validation. The adb client joins those arguments into a remote command string that the Android shell reparses, allowing shell metacharacters to execute additional commands on an authorized connected device as the Android shell user. Exploitation requires a valid Mobile MCP API key and a reachable device authorized for ADB, and it does not establish host operating-system execution, Android root execution, or access beyond the Android shell-user privileges. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.10.

cna.title: Plane: SSRF via HTTP redirect in webhook delivery (allow_redirects not set)

descriptions.value: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, the webhook delivery task in apps/api/plane/bgtasks/webhook_task.py calls requests.post() without allow_redirects=False and does not validate redirect targets. validate_url() blocks private, loopback, link-local, and reserved addresses in the original webhook URL, but the final URL reached after one or more redirects is not checked. A user who can create a workspace can register a webhook pointing to an attacker-controlled public endpoint that returns a 302 redirect to an internal address. The Plane worker then fetches internal resources, including cloud metadata, and stores the response body in webhook_logs, where the attacker can retrieve it through the workspace webhook-logs API. This issue is fixed in 1.4.0.

workarounds.value:
How To Apply the Fix

  *  Open the OpenShift console and navigate to Administration > CustomResourceDefinitions. 
  *  Search for coreidp.
  *  Show coreidp instances.
  *  Select the instance associated with your MAS installation;
  *  Edit Coreidp CR for your instance with the following under spec.settings field:
  *  Under the spec.settings field, add the following configuration, replacing <version> with the value specified in the table above for your MAS release:


spec:
  settings:
    imageTags:
      coreidplogin: <version>


  *  Save the change. This will trigger the Coreidp Entity Manager operator to reconcile and recreate the coreidp-login deployment automatically.
  *  Wait for the new deployment to become ready, then follow the validation steps below. 

IMPORTANT: Only remove the imageTags override from the Suite settings AFTER updating to the October 2026 monthly update or later, as earlier versions do not include the fix. Removing it before that point will revert your installation to the vulnerable version.

The verifier has no per-code failed-attempt counter, and an incorrect code does not increment a counter, invalidate the Redis entry, or lock the email address. The verifier extends django.views.View rather than DRF's APIView, so the configured AnonRateThrottle limit does not apply. The middleware stack also contains no Django-level rate limiter such as django-ratelimit, django-axes, or an IP-throttling middleware. This vulnerability is fixed in 1.4.0.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the Dynamic Client Registration flow of the Keycloak identity and access management server. descriptions.value: go-micro before 6.0.0 contains an improper certificate validation vulnerability that allows network attackers to impersonate services because the shared TLS helper sets InsecureSkipVerify to true by default. Man-in-the-middle attackers can present any certificate to intercept or modify gRPC transport, HTTP and RabbitMQ broker, and Consul or etcd registry traffic, including authentication tokens and credentials.

rejectedReasons.value: This candidate was rejected after further investigation determined that it is not a security vulnerability. The client certificate chain is validated during mTLS negotiation at the TLS layer or reverse proxy before Keycloak processes CRL Distribution Point or OCSP URLs, so only certificates issued by a CA explicitly trusted by the administrator can trigger these requests.

descriptions.value: An unauthenticated client can make the application see any host string and any port number as the request's authority, bypassing the validation applied to the Host header. descriptions.value:
Improper Validation of Syntactic Correctness of Input vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to set conn.host and conn.port to values outside the RFC 3986 host grammar via the authority of an HTTP/1 absolute-form or authority-form request target. Bandit validates the Host header and answers 400 when it is malformed, but when the request target carries its own authority that authority takes precedence, as RFC 9112 requires, and Bandit.Pipeline.determine_host_and_port!/4 in lib/bandit/pipeline.ex passes it to the application unchecked. A request line such as GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.1 with a valid Host header yields a conn.host of good.example@evil.example, and the same path admits NUL, DEL and non-ASCII bytes, invalid IP literals and ports outside 1..65535. The HTTP/1.0 clause needs no Host header at all, and CONNECT places the unparsed port string in conn.port.

Applications that build absolute URLs from conn.host, such as through Plug.Conn.request_url/1 or Phoenix URL helpers, emit links whose authority the attacker chose. Message framing is unaffected, and no CR or LF can reach conn.host.

This issue affects bandit: from 0.6.0 before 1.13.0.

x_proofOfConcept.value:
* Start Bandit over plaintext HTTP with a plug that returns conn.host and conn.port.
* Open a raw TCP connection to the listener and send GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.1 followed by Host: good.example and an empty line. The response is 200 and conn.host is good.example@evil.example.
* Repeat with GET http://ex\x00am.com/x HTTP/1.1 (a NUL byte in the authority) or GET http://ex.com:99999/x HTTP/1.1. Both are accepted, with the NUL byte in conn.host and 99999 in conn.port.
* Send the same bytes in the Host header of an origin-form request instead. Bandit answers 400 for the NUL byte and the out-of-range port on 1.12.5, and for every payload once the Host grammar tightening on main is released.
* Send GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.0 with no Host header, or CONNECT good.example@evil.example:443 HTTP/1.1. Both are accepted, and the CONNECT form leaves conn.port as the binary "443".

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Request-target parsing (lib/bandit/http1/socket.ex)

:erlang.decode_packet/3 returns an absolute-form target as {:absoluteURI, scheme, host, port, path} and an authority-form (CONNECT) target as {:scheme, host, port}. resolve_request_target!/2 unwraps both into a {scheme, host, port, path} tuple and forwards host and port as received. validate_request_line!/2 only rejects bytes at or below 0x20 and 0x7F, so userinfo, delimiters, backslashes, bytes 0x80 to 0xFF, invalid IP literals and out-of-range ports pass. For CONNECT, port is the unparsed text after the first colon.

2. Host selection (lib/bandit/pipeline.ex)

determine_host_and_port!/4 has three clauses. The HTTP/1.1 clause calls required_host_header!/1, which parses the Host header with Bandit.Headers.parse_hostlike_header!/1 and raises a 400 on a malformed value, and then discards that result whenever target_host is set, returning to_string(target_host) and target_port instead. The fallback clause used for HTTP/1.0 and for CONNECT returns the target host and port directly and never consults the Host header. The precedence itself follows RFC 9112 section 3.2.2; the defect is that the value which wins is the one never validated.

3. Effect

build_conn!/6 places the pair into the URI from which Plug.Conn.Adapter.conn/5 builds conn.host and conn.port. The application therefore sees host values Bandit rejects on every other route into the same field, and for CONNECT a binary where Plug.Conn.port_number/0 promises an integer, which makes Plug.Conn.request_url/1 raise.

**1. Request-target parsing** (`lib/bandit/http1/socket.ex`)

`:erlang.decode_packet/3` returns an absolute-form target as `{:absoluteURI, scheme, host, port, path}` and an authority-form (`CONNECT`) target as `{:scheme, host, port}`. `resolve_request_target!/2` unwraps both into a `{scheme, host, port, path}` tuple and forwards `host` and `port` as received. `validate_request_line!/2` only rejects bytes at or below `0x20` and `0x7F`, so userinfo, delimiters, backslashes, bytes `0x80` to `0xFF`, invalid IP literals and out-of-range ports pass. For `CONNECT`, `port` is the unparsed text after the first colon.

**2. Host selection** (`lib/bandit/pipeline.ex`)

`determine_host_and_port!/4` has three clauses. The HTTP/1.1 clause calls `required_host_header!/1`, which parses the `Host` header with `Bandit.Headers.parse_hostlike_header!/1` and raises a 400 on a malformed value, and then discards that result whenever `target_host` is set, returning `to_string(target_host)` and `target_port` instead. The fallback clause used for HTTP/1.0 and for `CONNECT` returns the target host and port directly and never consults the `Host` header. The precedence itself follows RFC 9112 section 3.2.2; the defect is that the value which wins is the one never validated.

**3. Effect**

`build_conn!/6` places the pair into the `URI` from which `Plug.Conn.Adapter.conn/5` builds `conn.host` and `conn.port`. The application therefore sees host values Bandit rejects on every other route into the same field, and for `CONNECT` a binary where `Plug.Conn.port_number/0` promises an integer, which makes `Plug.Conn.request_url/1` raise.

cna.title: Vault ACL Policy Cache Vulnerable to Cross-Namespace Policy Resolution

credits.value: This issue was identified by an external party.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-126: Path Traversal

Vault's ACL policy cache allowed namespace traversal when policy names contained path traversal constructs. This may allow a token assigned specially crafted policy names to use the capabilities of policies defined in other namespaces, including the root namespace. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-105820) is fixed in Vault Enterprise 2.1.2, 1.21.12, 1.20.17, and 1.19.23. Vault Community Edition does not support namespaces, and is not affected.

cna.title: Cups: cups: argument injection in mailto notifier via notify-recipient-uri

workarounds.value: Restrict network access to the CUPS service (port 631/tcp) to trusted hosts only, and avoid exposing cupsd to untrusted networks. If email notifications are not required, do not configure mailto subscriptions or remove/disable the mailto notifier. Ensure only a trusted mail transfer agent is installed and referenced from CUPS mailto configuration. Monitor for unexpected printer subscriptions and unusual sendmail activity from the lp user.

descriptions.value: An argument injection flaw was found in CUPS. When email notification is configured, the CUPS scheduler accepts printer subscription requests that supply a mailto notify-recipient-uri. The mailto notifier passes the recipient address to the configured sendmail program without ensuring it cannot be interpreted as command-line options. A remote attacker who can reach the CUPS service could supply a crafted recipient value starting with "-" to influence sendmail behavior. Successful exploitation depends on the installed mail transfer agent and CUPS network exposure, and may lead to execution of attacker-controlled commands with the privileges of the CUPS service user.

cna.title: Penpot: Missing authorization in chunked-upload assembly lets another authenticated user consume a victim's upload session

descriptions.value: Penpot is an open-source design and prototyping platform. Prior to 2.18.0, assemble-chunks retrieves an upload session using only its session ID, while upload-chunk correctly scopes the lookup to the authenticated profile. An authenticated user who obtains another user's live, completed upload-session UUID can assemble the victim's chunks into the attacker's own file, team font, or project import, disclosing the uploaded bytes and deleting the victim's pending session. This issue is fixed in version 2.18.0.

cna.title: hex_core decompresses registry and Erlang term API responses without size limits

descriptions.value: A mirror can make every registry fetch allocate memory far beyond the size of its response: in a test against Hex main 851b938, which vendors this code, a 65 KB registry response decompressed into a 64 MiB envelope before the signature check failed. The API server, or an attacker who can alter its responses, can do the same with API responses: 8 KB of compressed Erlang term format decoded into a list of 4.2 million elements. Large enough responses stop the Erlang VM, which fails the build tool command or the program using hex_core. No package code has to run.

descriptions.value:
Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) vulnerability in hexpm hex_core allows an untrusted repository mirror, or a server answering hex_core's API requests, to exhaust the memory of the Erlang VM running hex_core. The same code is vendored in Hex (mix_hex_repo, mix_hex_api) and rebar3 (r3_hex_repo, r3_hex_api).

hex_repo:get_names/1, hex_repo:get_versions/1, hex_repo:get_package/2 and hex_repo:get_policy/2 decompress the registry response with zlib:gunzip/1 and decode the signed envelope before verifying its signature. A mirror doesn't have the repository's private key, but it chooses the compressed bytes, so a small response decompresses into an envelope of any size before the signature check rejects it.

hex_api decodes responses with the application/vnd.hex+erlang content type through hex_safe_binary_to_term:safe_binary_to_term/1, which calls binary_to_term(Binary, [safe]). The safe option prevents atom creation, but it accepts compressed terms and doesn't limit the size of the decoded term, and the check that rejects functions and ports runs after the term has been built. The fix for CVE-2026-21619 added the safe option and that check without bounding the decoded size.

This issue affects rebar3: from 3.9.1 before 3.27.3; hex: from 2.1.0 before 2.5.2; hex_core: from 0.1.0 before 0.20.0.

solutions.value:
Mitigation:

  *

descriptions.value:
Summary



Before version 0.9.0, Pingora accepted HTTP/2 requests whose Host header differed from the :authority pseudo-header. Request filters, cache keys, and logs that read the request URI (session.req_header().uri) saw the :authority value, but the upstream received the client-supplied Host value. Pingora also accepted :authority values containing userinfo (for example, user@example.com). This violates RFC 9113 Section 8.3.1, which requires an intermediary to use the :authority value for Host and replace any existing Host field.




Root cause

  *  

HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1: Host was generated from :authority only when the request had no Host header, so a conflicting client Host was forwarded unchanged.


  *  

HTTP/2 to HTTP/2: the client Host header was removed and used to overwrite the upstream :authority, after request filters had already run against the original :authority.


  *  

The HTTP/2 server did not compare Host with :authority and did not reject userinfo in the authority.







Impact



A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a single HTTP/2 request that the application sees as one host and the upstream receives as another. Where request filters, access controls, or cache keys use the URI authority and the upstream routes by Host, this can lead to:

  *  

Cache poisoning: a response from another virtual host is stored under the victim host's cache key and served to other users (this also requires the upstream to serve different content per Host).


  *  

Host-based access control bypass: a request approved for one host is served by a different virtual host on the upstream.






Deployments that do not accept HTTP/2 from clients, or that do not use the request authority for security or caching decisions, are not affected.




Note that Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as internal Pingora services at Cloudflare do not have HTTP/2 clients.




Mitigation:

  *  

Upgrade to pingora 0.9.0 or later. Pingora now returns 400 Bad Request for HTTP/2 requests whose Host differs from :authority, that contain more than one Host, or whose authority contains userinfo, and keeps the upstream Host or :authority consistent with the request authority. Fix commits:  https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/commit/915590a91811877795531f6ba0927a3138b5cb4b ,  https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/commit/ffab8302d08d4292d1924eb8fe84647fd5cb8e76 


  *  

If you cannot upgrade: in request_filter, reject HTTP/2 requests that carry a Host header different from the URI authority, or whose authority contains '@'.

descriptions.value: Langflow is a tool for building and deploying AI-powered agents and workflows. cna.title: Cruise-control: streams for apache kafka cruise control: authentication bypass via extra path segment allows unauthenticated access to all admin endpoints

workarounds.value:
1. Verify Strimzi NetworkPolicy exists restricting CC :9090 to operator pods
2. Do not expose CC :9090 via Ingress or Route — must not be externally accessible
3. Confirm TLS is enabled on the CC HTTP endpoint (Strimzi default)
4. For standalone CC: deploy path-normalizing reverse proxy and restrict :9090 via firewall

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to eliminate the path discrepancy between Jetty security constraints and ParameterUtils routing by canonicalizing URI paths prior to authorization evaluation: upgrade to the fixed Cruise Control/Kafka Relations Sink/Playbook Dispatcher/Cloudservices/Kafka Relations Sink/Redhat User Workloads/Playbook Dispatcher Connect builds, which canonicalizes request URI paths prior to authorization and registers wildcard security constraints or denies uncovered HTTP methods in Jetty, closing prepending an arbitrary path segment to administrative endpoint URIs. Until patched, this is a concern on Cruise Control deployments exposing HTTP port 9090 without network policy restrictions or reverse proxy path filtering, so Enforce Strimzi NetworkPolicy restricting port 9090 access strictly to operator pods, prohibit external exposure through Ingress or Routes, and deploy a path-normalizing reverse proxy or firewall rules for standalone setups. As a compensating measure, Require authenticated identity verification at the network boundary using a zero trust gateway or identity-aware proxy before traffic reaches port 9090, Restrict network access to Cruise Control port 9090 using host-based firewalls like firewalld or nftables, Bind the Cruise Control service to localhost to ensure all incoming traffic passes through a local tunnel or controlling reverse proxy, Enforce URL path authorization rules at an upstream reverse proxy to block unmapped or manipulated URI paths, and Forward Cruise Control administrative endpoint invocations to a SIEM to detect unauthorized execution of admin actions. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying path discrepancy authentication bypass defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-921 URL Request Path Canonicalization Before Authorization (high)

descriptions.value: Cruise Control's Jetty ConstraintSecurityHandler registers security constraints on exact path specs without a catch-all wildcard constraint and without calling setDenyUncoveredHttpMethods(true). The servlet routes requests using Path.of(pathInfo).getFileName(), which strips all leading segments and trailing slashes. Requests like POST /kafkacruisecontrol/x/rebalance bypass authentication entirely but still dispatch to admin endpoints. All 15 admin endpoints become reachable without authentication. In AMQ Streams, the Strimzi operator's NetworkPolicy restricts Cruise Control port 9090 to operator pods only, reducing effective severity to Important.

cna.title: Koha SQL injection in reports/cat_issues_top.pl via the Criteria, Filter and Limit request parameters

descriptions.value: Koha is vulnerable to SQL injection in the Most-circulated items report. The reports/cat_issues_top.pl script (sub calculate) concatenates the user-controlled Criteria, Filter, and Limit request parameters directly into dynamic SQL. Criteria is only prefix-normalized and never validated against an allow-list, so it is inserted verbatim into identifier positions (SELECT DISTINCTROW, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, and the main calculation query). Filter values are concatenated raw into single-quoted LIKE, BETWEEN, and comparison fragments. Limit is appended raw to a LIMIT clause. An authenticated staff user with the reports module permission (not requiring superlibrarian) can inject arbitrary SQL and read any table reachable by the Koha database user, including borrowers (userid and bcrypt password hashes, two-factor secrets, personal data), api_keys, and sessions. The issue is fixed in Koha 24.11.19, 25.05.14, 25.11.08, and 26.05.03, and in the 26.11 development branch. This is the unpatched twin of reports/bor_issues_top.pl (CVE-2026-70372).

cna.title: Unauthenticated ZeroMQ command/telemetry bus in AIT-Core allows remote spacecraft command injection and telemetry exfiltration

descriptions.value: With the shipped default configuration, the ZeroMQ command and telemetry bus is unauthenticated and network-reachable because ait-server binds to all network interfaces. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach TCP ports 5559 or 5560 can inject arbitrary data onto the spacecraft command-uplink path, read real-time telemetry and command traffic from the ground bus, inject forged telemetry into operator displays, limit checks, and the historian, or disrupt command-bus availability. Exploitation requires no plugin, credentials, or user interaction; ait-server only needs to be running and the affected ZeroMQ ports must be reachable. Successful exploitation compromises the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the spacecraft command and telemetry path.

solutions.value: Upgrade to AIT-Core 3.1.2 or later. Version 3.1.2 changes the default ZeroMQ XSUB and XPUB bind addresses to loopback. Deployments that require the ZeroMQ message bus to operate across multiple hosts should protect the bus using authenticated and encrypted transport such as ZeroMQ CURVE or an equivalent mutually authenticated TLS-protected network layer.

descriptions.value: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function in the ait.core.server telemetry and command broker (ait-server) in NASA-AMMOS AIT-Core through 3.1.1 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker with network access to the ZeroMQ message bus to inject spacecraft command data, exfiltrate command and telemetry traffic, inject forged telemetry, or disrupt the command and telemetry bus. The ait-server ZeroMQ broker binds its XSUB and XPUB sockets to all network interfaces by default without authentication or transport security. An attacker able to reach TCP port 5559 can publish messages onto internal topics, including the __commands__ command topic. With the shipped default configuration, command messages are forwarded through command_stream and emitted on the command-uplink UDP path. cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Missing topic policy authorization on non-persistent topic entry filter endpoints

credits.value: Mingsheng Lin of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Xingchen Chen of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Qixu Liu of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS

descriptions.value:
The Apache Pulsar broker admin REST API provides endpoints to read, set and remove the topic-level entry filter policy of a topic. For persistent topics these endpoints check that the caller is authorized for the entry filters topic policy operation. The corresponding endpoints for non-persistent topics (/admin/v2/non-persistent/{tenant}/{namespace}/{topic}/entryFilters) do not perform this authorization check. The only authorization check these endpoints perform is an indirect lookup permission check, made while the topic's partition metadata is retrieved; it is present in all affected versions.

As a result, when authentication and authorization are enabled, an authenticated user who has been granted produce or consume permission on a non-persistent topic, or on its namespace, but not permission to manage the topic's policies can read, replace or remove the topic-level entry filter policy of that topic. These operations should be restricted to users with the tenant admin role or the superuser role. This impact analysis assumes that Pulsar has been configured with the default authorization provider. For custom authorization providers, the impact could be slightly different.

The practical impact is limited by two broker configuration requirements, neither of which is met by default:

- Entry filters must have been installed by the operator. Entry filter implementations are loaded only at broker startup from the broker's entry filters directory, which is empty by default. A request can only select among entry filters the operator has already deployed; setting any other filter name is rejected. The issue does not allow a caller to install or load entry filter code or to run arbitrary code in the broker.
- Topic-level entry filter policies must be allowed to override the broker-level configuration (allowOverrideEntryFilters, which is disabled by default). When this setting is disabled, the topic-level entry filter policy has no effect on message dispatch.

In deployments where both conditions are met, an unauthorized user can remove the topic-level entry filter policy of a non-persistent topic, for example one used to restrict which messages are delivered to consumers, or apply a different installed entry filter that withholds messages from subscriptions of that topic. Removing it makes the topic fall back to the namespace-level or broker-level entry filters, which are not removed. A changed policy affects only subscription dispatchers created after the change, for example for new subscriptions or when a subscription is re-created after all of its consumers have disconnected; dispatchers that already exist keep the entry filters they were created with. Because non-persistent topics do not store messages, messages withheld by an entry filter are not delivered. Reading the policy discloses only the names of the configured entry filters. The issue does not allow reading message contents, and entry filters cannot modify message payloads. Persistent topics and namespace-level entry filter policies are not affected. Apache Pulsar versions before 3.3.0 are not affected, because in those versions the entry filters topic policy check is made in code shared by the persistent and non-persistent endpoints.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 3.3.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 3.3.x and 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately and have deployed entry filters should keep allowOverrideEntryFilters at its default value of false, so that topic-level entry filter policies do not affect message dispatch.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Subscription authorization policies not enforced by namespace-level backlog and unsubscribe operations and by topic expire-all

descriptions.value:
Apache Pulsar namespaces can restrict which roles may use a subscription, either with the Prefix subscription authentication mode, which requires a subscription name to start with the role name, or by granting permission on a subscription to specific roles. Topic-level subscription operations, such as consuming, skipping messages, resetting a cursor or deleting a subscription, apply these subscription policies. Several admin REST API operations that act on subscriptions did not apply them:

- the namespace-level and bundle-level clear backlog operations, both for a named subscription and for all subscriptions;
- the namespace-level and bundle-level unsubscribe operations;
- the topic-level operation that expires messages for all subscriptions of a topic.

With the default authorization provider, the namespace-level operations require only consume permission granted on the namespace, and the expire-all operation requires only consume permission on the topic. As a result, when authentication and authorization are enabled and a namespace uses the Prefix subscription authentication mode or subscription permissions, an authenticated user with such consume permission can clear the backlog of, expire messages of, or delete a subscription that the policies would deny to that user. Tenant admin or superuser access is not required. The clear backlog operations can also be applied to the cursors used for geo-replication, so that messages not yet replicated to a remote cluster are skipped. Deployments that do not configure the Prefix subscription authentication mode or subscription permissions (the defaults) are not affected by this bypass, because consume permission on the namespace or topic already allows these operations there. This impact analysis assumes that Pulsar has been configured with the default authorization provider. For custom authorization providers, the impact could be different.

The impact is on the integrity of subscription state. Clearing or expiring the backlog moves the subscription's cursor forward, so unacknowledged messages are no longer delivered to the subscription's consumers. The unsubscribe operation deletes a subscription that has no connected consumers. Skipped messages can be permanently deleted once no other subscription or the namespace's retention policy keeps them. The issue does not allow reading message contents, changing permissions or policies, or accessing other namespaces, and it does not affect the availability of the broker.

In fixed versions, the namespace-level and bundle-level operations for a named subscription apply the subscription policies to that subscription, and the operations for all subscriptions, when requested by a user who is not a tenant admin or superuser, only act on the subscriptions that the user may access. Clearing the backlog of geo-replication cursors requires tenant admin or superuser access. Topic-level subscription operations apply the subscription policies for all types of authentication data, including that of the anonymous user role.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

All brokers in a cluster must be upgraded before relying on the namespace-level restrictions, because brokers that have not been upgraded do not apply them when they receive the internal per-bundle requests.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately can reduce exposure by restricting network access to the broker's admin REST API to trusted administrative clients.

As a result, when authentication and authorization are enabled and a namespace uses the Prefix subscription authentication mode or subscription permissions, an authenticated user with such consume permission can clear the backlog of, expire messages of, or delete a subscription that the policies would deny to that user. Tenant admin or superuser access is not required. The clear backlog operations can also be applied to the cursors used for geo-replication, so that messages not yet replicated to a remote cluster are skipped. Deployments that do not configure the Prefix subscription authentication mode or subscription permissions (the defaults) are not affected by this bypass, because consume permission on the namespace or topic already allows these operations there. This impact analysis assumes that Pulsar has been configured with the default authorization provider. For custom authorization providers, the impact could be different.

The impact is on the integrity of subscription state. Clearing or expiring the backlog moves the subscription's cursor forward, so unacknowledged messages are no longer delivered to the subscription's consumers. The unsubscribe operation deletes a subscription that has no connected consumers. Skipped messages can be permanently deleted once no other subscription or the namespace's retention policy keeps them. The issue does not allow reading message contents, changing permissions or policies, or accessing other namespaces, and it does not affect the availability of the broker.

In fixed versions, the namespace-level and bundle-level operations for a named subscription apply the subscription policies to that subscription, and the operations for all subscriptions, when requested by a user who is not a tenant admin or superuser, only act on the subscriptions that the user may access. Clearing the backlog of geo-replication cursors requires tenant admin or superuser access. Topic-level subscription operations apply the subscription policies for all types of authentication data, including that of the anonymous user role.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

All brokers in a cluster must be upgraded before relying on the namespace-level restrictions, because brokers that have not been upgraded do not apply them when they receive the internal per-bundle requests.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately can reduce exposure by restricting network access to the broker's admin REST API to trusted administrative clients.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Function trigger publishes to the input topic without checking the caller's produce permission

descriptions.value:
The Pulsar Functions Worker provides a REST API endpoint for triggering a function, which publishes a caller-supplied value to one of the function's configured input topics. The Functions Worker performs this publish with its own broker client, which authenticates with the Worker's configured broker-client credentials rather than the credentials of the API caller.

When authorization is enabled, in Apache Pulsar 2.4.0 and later versions, the trigger endpoint checks only that the caller is authorized to perform function operations in the function's namespace. It does not check that the caller is authorized to produce to the input topic that the message is published to. Versions before 2.4.0 do not perform a caller authorization check for the trigger endpoint at all. Function input topics are not restricted to the function's own tenant or namespace, and registering a function does not require produce permission on its input topics.

As a result, an authenticated user who is authorized to manage functions in a namespace, for example a role granted the functions permission on that namespace, can cause the Functions Worker to publish messages with caller-controlled content to a topic that the user is not authorized to produce to, including topics in other tenants. These messages are published under the identity of the Functions Worker. The issue does not require any function instance to be running or any function code to be executed. It requires that the Functions Worker's broker-client identity is itself authorized to produce to the target topic and, in Apache Pulsar 2.3.0 and later versions, to list the subscriptions of the target topic, as is the case when that identity is a superuser. The impact is on the integrity of the data in the affected topics: consumers of those topics may receive messages from a user who is not permitted to publish them. This concerns the Functions Worker REST API as called by an external, authenticated client; it does not change the security model for function code, which must be fully trusted.

In fixed versions, when authorization is enabled, triggering a function additionally requires the caller to be authorized to produce to the selected input topic before any message is published.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.0.0-rc1-incubating before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users of Apache Pulsar 2.4.0 and later versions with authorization enabled who cannot upgrade immediately can limit the permission to manage functions to trusted roles. Users of versions before 2.4.0 should restrict access to the Functions Worker REST API to trusted callers, because in these versions the trigger endpoint does not check the caller's permission to manage functions.

cna.title: Spice-server: spice: heap oob read/write via unchecked migration data offsets

credits.value: Upstream acknowledges Tristan Madani (Talence Security) as the original reporter.

workarounds.value:
This vulnerability is only exploitable during VM live migration by an authenticated SPICE client. If live migration is not required, disabling it eliminates the attack surface. If live migration is needed, restrict SPICE client connections to trusted networks using firewall rules and enforce strong authentication (TLS with mutual certificate validation, or SASL with strong credentials) to limit who can connect as a SPICE client.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to enforce strict bounds validation on client-supplied offsets and buffer lengths across all SPICE migration data handlers prior to memory operations: upgrade to the fixed Spice/Spice Server builds, which validate migration data offsets and read bounds against declared message lengths instead of reallocating from attacker-controlled values, closing all 4 injection vectors (RedCharDevice restore via write_data_ptr offset manipulation, smartcard restore via read_data_ptr offset manipulation, reds agent state restore via msg_header_ptr offset manipulation, DisplayChannelClient migrate data handling via surfaces_at_client_ptr offset manipulation). Until patched, this is a concern on Linux hosts running Spice Server with VM live migration enabled, so disable VM live migration if not required, restrict SPICE client network access using firewall rules, and enforce strong authentication via SASL or mutual TLS. As a compensating measure, randomize heap and binary addresses using ASLR to impede reliable exploitation of out-of-bounds reads and writes, enforce full RELRO and PIE to make Global Offset Table entries read-only and prevent control flow diversion via heap corruption, validate indirect call targets using Control Flow Integrity or shadow call stacks to block redirection upon corruption of function pointers or vtables, enable FORTIFY_SOURCE to detect buffer overflows during memory copy operations such as memcpy and abort execution, and confine the SPICE server process using SELinux in enforcing mode to restrict host access if arbitrary code execution occurs. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying unchecked migration data offsets defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-301 SELinux (Enforcing Mode) (medium)

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in spice-server. Multiple migration data handlers use client-supplied offsets from SPICE_MSGC_MIGRATE_DATA messages without bounds validation, allowing a malicious authenticated SPICE client during VM live migration to read arbitrary heap memory or trigger heap corruption via out-of-bounds read and write operations on the message buffer.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Improper Authorization of Function, Source and Sink Package URLs Allows Cross-Tenant Package Download

descriptions.value:
When package management is enabled, Pulsar Functions, Sources and Sinks can be registered or updated from a package stored in the Pulsar Packages Management Service by supplying a package URL. The Pulsar Functions worker authorized these requests only against the namespace in which the component was being registered or updated. It did not check whether the requesting user was permitted to access packages in the namespace that the package URL refers to, and it retrieved the package from the broker using the worker's own credentials. The permission check of the Packages Management Service was therefore applied to the worker's identity instead of the requesting user's. Package URLs of transform functions supplied when registering or updating a sink were handled in the same way.

An authenticated user who is permitted to register or update functions, sources or sinks in any namespace of their own tenant could use this to obtain the contents of a package stored in a namespace of another tenant, without having the packages permission on that namespace. The impact is limited to disclosure of package contents, which may include application code, business logic or embedded credentials. The issue does not allow packages to be modified or deleted and does not affect availability.

This issue only affects deployments that have authentication and authorization enabled and in which package management has been enabled: the broker setting enablePackagesManagement and, in current releases, the functions worker setting functionsWorkerEnablePackageManagement. Both settings are disabled by default.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.0 before 4.0.14, from 4.1.0 through 4.1.3, and from 4.2.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

cna.title: HTTP/2 blocked-send deadlines reset on every WINDOW_UPDATE, letting a trickle pin stream processes indefinitely in Bandit

descriptions.value: A remote, unauthenticated peer requests a response larger than a send window, then drips tiny WINDOW_UPDATE frames every few seconds. Each blocked stream process, with its Plug state and any upstream connection or file handle it holds, stays alive for as long as the trickle continues. Repeated across many streams and connections this exhausts server processes and memory.

descriptions.value:
Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to pin HTTP/2 stream processes indefinitely via a trickle of small WINDOW_UPDATE frames. A stream whose response outruns the connection or stream send window blocks until the peer grants more window, and each block carries a 15 second deadline. Both deadlines restart whenever the peer makes partial progress. Bandit.HTTP2.Connection.finish_data/5 re-queues a partially advanced send in pending_sends with a fresh expires_at, so every WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0, and every SETTINGS frame, resets the clock. Bandit.HTTP2.Stream.send_data/3 recurses on each stream WINDOW_UPDATE and re-arms a fresh after read_timeout. A peer that grants a few bytes every few seconds keeps the blocked stream process, its Plug state and any resource it holds mid-response alive for as long as it keeps dripping, and repeats this across streams and connections to exhaust server processes and memory.

The two paths are independent. The stream-level block is reached on its own by widening the connection window with a large WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0 and shrinking the per-stream window with a small SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE, so closing only the connection-level path leaves it exploitable.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.4.0 before 1.13.0.

* The server sends the window's worth and queues the remainder in pending_sends.
* Send WINDOW_UPDATE for stream 0 with an increment of 1 every few seconds, or an empty SETTINGS frame. Each one re-queues the remainder with a fresh deadline, so expire_pending_sends/1 never expires it.

Stream-level path:

* Send a large WINDOW_UPDATE for stream 0 so the connection window never blocks.
* Advertise a small SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE so each stream window is tiny.
* Request a response larger than the stream window. The server sends the window's worth and blocks in the recursive receive in send_data/3.
* Send WINDOW_UPDATE for the stream with an increment of 1 at intervals shorter than 15 seconds. Each one re-arms a fresh read_timeout.
* Repeat across streams, up to max_concurrent_streams per connection, and across connections.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Connection-level block (lib/bandit/http2/connection.ex)

A send that outruns the connection send window is queued in pending_sends with an expires_at deadline computed in finish_data/5 as now plus @pending_send_timeout (15 seconds). expire_pending_sends/1 drops any queued send whose deadline has passed whenever data arrives on the connection. do_pending_sends/2 runs on every WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0 and on every SETTINGS frame (including an empty one, through handle_frame/3). When the granted window is smaller than the queued remainder, the leftover is re-queued through finish_data/5, which recomputes expires_at from the current time instead of preserving the original deadline. Each partial advance therefore restarts the timer, and an empty SETTINGS frame restarts it without granting any window at all.

2. Stream-level block (lib/bandit/http2/stream.ex)

send_data/3 runs in the stream process. When the stream send window is exhausted it enters a receive that waits for {:bandit, {:send_window_update, delta}} with after stream.read_timeout (the struct default of 15 seconds, never overridden in init/5). On each stream WINDOW_UPDATE it applies the delta and recurses into send_data/3 with the remainder, which re-enters the same receive with a fresh after timeout. Each partial advance restarts the 15 second wait.

For the stream-level block to be the one stuck, the stream window must be exhausted while the connection window has room. The peer controls both: a large WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0 opens the connection window, and a small SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE shrinks every stream window. Closing only the connection-level path therefore leaves the stream-level path fully exploitable.

3. Effect

The trickle also keeps the transport-level read timeout from firing, since the connection continuously receives valid frames. The blocked stream process, its Plug state, and anything it holds mid-response stay retained for as long as the peer keeps dripping, instead of being released after 15 seconds.

cna.title: Kroxylicious-kms-provider-azure-key-vault-kms: streams for apache kafka kroxylicious: azure key vault ssrf exfiltrates bearer token via untrusted edek vaultname

workarounds.value:
1. Restrict outbound network access — use Kubernetes NetworkPolicy to limit proxy pod egress to only legitimate Azure Key Vault endpoints on port 443.
2. Monitor KMS call patterns — alert on unwrap requests targeting unexpected vault hostnames.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to enforce strict allowlist regex validation on wire-deserialized vaultName in the Azure Key Vault KMS provider before constructing outbound HTTP endpoints: upgrade to kroxylicious-kms-provider-azure-key-vault-kms 0.25.1+ (or the fixed Kroxylicious Kms Provider Azure Key Vault Kms builds), which validate Key Vault name using validateKeyVaultName to reject names containing dots, URL fragments, invalid lengths, or malformed hyphens before constructing the Key Vault URL, closing all 2 injection vectors (crafted EDEK containing an arbitrary hostname in vaultName, vaultName URL fragment injection). Until patched, this is a concern on Kafka clusters using the Kroxylicious Record Encryption filter with Azure Key Vault KMS, so restrict proxy pod outbound network egress using Kubernetes NetworkPolicy strictly to legitimate Azure Key Vault endpoints on port 443 and alert on unwrap requests targeting unexpected vault hostnames. As a compensating measure, Deploy Falco or eBPF runtime security to detect anomalous outbound network connections initiated by the Kroxylicious proxy process to unexpected destinations. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying unvalidated input SSRF defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-1315 Allowlist-Preferred Input Validation (Deny-by-Default Filtering) (high)

descriptions.value: The Azure Key Vault KMS provider in Kroxylicious accepts an untrusted vaultName from wire-deserialized EDEK bytes without format validation, enabling SSRF that exfiltrates the proxy's Azure bearer token to an attacker-controlled host. Token replay against the real Key Vault defeats the entire record-encryption trust model.

session.

perform protected camera operations, including pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) control,
without a valid authenticated session. This could result in unauthorized
manipulation of camera functionality.

From 2.95.0 until 2.132.0, the HTML image resource loader in docling/backend/utils/image_resource_loader.py forwards headers configured through the HTMLBackendOptions.headers setting to every remote image URL named by an untrusted document when enable_remote_fetch=True and fetch_images=True. The loader does not restrict those credentials to the source document's origin, allowing requests that carry custom headers such as API keys and cookies to follow cross-origin redirects and expose the caller's configured credentials to a document author. The proxy removed alternate credentials only when their values matched known sentinel values, so untrusted code in an authorized sandbox could supply an unrecognized credential in another supported authentication header. For affected upstream services, this could authenticate the request to an attacker-controlled account and expose data included in the request.

supportingMedia.value:
Protection Mechanism Failure vulnerability in hexpm hex allows the owner of a package, or an attacker who has taken over the owner's account, to get a newly published release past the release-age cooldown.

The cooldown (cooldown config, HEX_COOLDOWN) withholds versions younger than the configured age during dependency resolution. When the release of a package locked in mix.lock is retired or has a security advisory, Hex.RemoteConverger.build_cooldown_bypass/3 and Hex.RemoteConverger.unsafe_lock_bypass/1 lift the cooldown for every version of that package and of every package the locked release depends on, so that mix deps.update can move off the unsafe release. Retiring a release needs the same package owner permission as publishing one. An attacker who publishes a malicious release can retire the currently locked release, and the next mix deps.update that unlocks the package selects the new release regardless of its age. Hex.Registry.Cooldown.versions/2 checks the bypass by package name alone, so the bypass also covers packages with the same name in other repositories. Cooldown configured through an organization dependency policy is not affected.

This issue affects hex: from 2.5.0 before 2.5.2.

supportingMedia.value: The cooldown exists to keep a compromised release out of projects until it can be detected and retired. An attacker who controls a package owner account can defeat it by also retiring the currently locked release, so a malicious release reaches projects that rely on the local cooldown as soon as they run mix deps.update, including automated dependency update jobs. The malicious release's code then runs when the dependency is compiled.

descriptions.value: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command in the integrate-platform-docs composite GitHub Action of Chainguard Academy (edu) from commit 7375a80caabcc31c33ec90f29687ed78c13d16ff before commit fb0efb2537d326ab18c07d620875b8ed2a4b39f3 allows an actor who controls the project_id or storage_bucket inputs to execute arbitrary shell commands on the GitHub Actions runner, because the inputs are interpolated directly into Bash gcloud storage cp commands in several steps via ${{ inputs.* }} expressions. cna.title: Docling: Crafted DoclingDocument JSON embeds local image files into converted output

descriptions.value: Docling simplifies document processing by parsing diverse formats and providing integrations with the generative AI ecosystem. From 2.16.0 until 2.131.0, the InputFormat.JSON_DOCLING backend in docling/backend/json/docling_json_backend.py validates serialized DoclingDocument input without rejecting picture image references that contain local paths or file URIs. When the document is enriched or exported with ImageRefMode.EMBEDDED, the DoclingDocument._with_embedded_pictures and ImageRef.pil_image methods can open those references and place readable image bytes in Markdown or HTML output. Disclosure is limited to files Pillow can decode as images, while differing decode behavior can also reveal whether a path exists. Direct untrusted loading through docling-core is outside this Docling fix. This issue is fixed in 2.131.0.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Functions connectors list endpoint does not apply the super-user check of the worker connectors endpoint

credits.value: Mingsheng Lin of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Xingchen Chen of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Qixu Liu of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS

descriptions.value:
The Pulsar Functions worker REST API provides two endpoints that return the catalog of Pulsar IO connectors installed on the functions worker: the worker connectors endpoint (/admin/v2/worker/connectors) and the deprecated functions connectors endpoint (/admin/v2/functions/connectors and /admin/v3/functions/connectors). When authorization is enabled, the worker connectors endpoint requires super-user access. The functions connectors endpoint, served both by the functions worker and by a broker running the functions worker, returns the same catalog without this check.

As a result, when authentication and authorization are enabled, any authenticated client can read the connector catalog through the functions connectors endpoint, regardless of the permissions granted to its role and without super-user access. Unauthenticated requests are rejected unless anonymous access is configured with an anonymous user role.

The catalog contains the connector type definitions installed in the functions worker's connectors directory: the connector name, its description, and the source, sink and configuration class names. It does not contain configured source or sink instances, their configuration values or credentials, and an installed connector type does not indicate that a connector is configured or running. The impact is limited to disclosure of this metadata, which can include the names and descriptions of custom connectors installed by the operator. The issue does not allow modifying the catalog or managing connectors. Connector definitions that have a source or sink class are also returned by the built-in sources and sinks endpoints to authenticated clients.

In fixed versions, the functions connectors endpoint applies the same checks as the worker connectors endpoint, so that it requires super-user access when authorization is enabled. Clients that are not super-users can use the built-in sources and sinks endpoints to list the available connector types.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.4.1 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

cna.title: TLS 1.2 session resumption in ssl crosses SNI virtual-host client-certificate trust boundaries

descriptions.value: A client holding a certificate issued by the lower-trust SNI name's CA connects to the higher-trust name as a fully authenticated mTLS peer and obtains whatever that service grants on a successful client-certificate handshake. Multi-tenant or partner-facing listeners that separate trust domains by SNI name are affected.

workarounds.value:
* Set {reuse_sessions, false} in each SNI service's option set, or in the base listener options. The reporter's proof of concept confirmed that this blocks the cross-name resumption.
* Serve distinct SNI trust domains on separate listen sockets, which gives each its own session cache.
* Restrict the listener to TLS 1.3 with {versions, ['tlsv1.3']}. TLS 1.3 does not use the session-ID cache.

descriptions.value:
Improper Certificate Validation vulnerability in the ssl application in Erlang/OTP allows a client that holds a certificate trusted by one SNI virtual host to authenticate to a second SNI virtual host on the same listener by resuming its TLS 1.2 session there.

A server that serves several SNI names from one listen socket through sni_fun or sni_hosts keeps one pre-TLS 1.3 session cache per listener and does not bind a cached session to the SNI name or client trust policy that established it. When an SNI option set switches to verify_peer without naming reuse_sessions, ssl_config:update_options/3 inherits the base listener's reuse_sessions value of true, so the default that disables reuse for client-authenticating servers does not apply. On an abbreviated handshake ssl_session:is_resumable/4 checks only that the cached session uses one of the current server certificates and carries some peer certificate, and never revalidates that certificate against the CA selected for the requested name. The names must share a server certificate, which is common with wildcard or multi-SAN certificates. TLS 1.3 does not use this cache and is not affected.

This issue affects OTP from OTP 18.0 before OTP 27.3.4.19, OTP 28.5.0.8, and OTP 29.1.2, corresponding to ssl from 7.0 before 11.2.12.14, 11.6.0.7, and 11.7.8.

x_proofOfConcept.value:
* Create one server certificate with subject alternative names low.test and high.test, two self-signed client CAs (low-ca, high-ca), and one client certificate signed by low-ca.
* Start an ssl:listen/2 server on TLS 1.2 with {verify, verify_none} and an sni_fun that returns {verify, verify_peer}, {fail_if_no_peer_cert, true} and the low-ca or high-ca cacertfile for the respective name. Do not set reuse_sessions anywhere.
* Connect with openssl s_client -servername high.test -tls1_2 -no_ticket using the low client certificate. The server rejects the handshake with unknown_ca.
* Connect with -servername low.test and the same certificate, saving the session with -sess_out. The handshake succeeds.
* Connect with -servername high.test and -sess_in pointing at the saved session. The server resumes the session, ssl:connection_information/2 reports session_resumption true for high.test, and the application behind the protected name serves the request to a client whose certificate high-ca never issued.
